title: Benji and the Seven Days
markdown:
Benji the gardener wrung his hands. His brow made a little wrinkle, the kind a blanket gets when someone sits on it wrong. He usually tucked his tiny seeds in, gentle as butterfly wings tickling the dirt. Today his brain felt like a bird’s nest full of buzzy bees.

“Which plant needs a drink today? And which one tomorrow?” He crouched by the peas. Their little leaves hung droopy-droopy. The proud petunias drooped too, even though they liked to stand tall and show off their pretty faces. “Which day is it for the giggling geraniums? I cannot remember.”

He sighed a gusty sigh that ruffled his already tousled hair. It sounded like a puff of wind trying to blow his thoughts into a neater pile and failing.

On a leaf so green it nearly sparkled sat Dot, a little red ladybird with seven shiny black spots. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Dot loved counting things. She saw Benji looking as if he had lost his favourite digging spade.

“Hmm,” she chirped, a tiny sound like a silver bell. “His plants look droopy. He looks lost.”

From his old tree, like a grandpa made of leaves and bark, Old Man Oakle whispered. His voice was a soft breeze through branches, not a whoosh meant for a crowd.

“Benji,” he murmured, a gentle rumble. “It is quite a job, looking after so many plants. Each one has its own thirst, its own time for a drink. A garden likes a schedule.”

Dot crawled closer to Benji’s shoe, legs wiggling. “Days,” she buzzed. “There are seven days. Just like my seven spots. Each day has a name. A code for the whole week.”

She thought of her spots, neat and round. “Monday. Tuesday. Wednesday. Then Thursday, Friday, and the weekend days, Saturday and Sunday. Each day a little bit special. A little bit different.”

Benji’s eyes, which had been so worried, popped open like blue marbles. “Days. Of course. The days of the week.” He had forgotten them in his busy planting. He laughed once, at himself, and the laugh made room for a plan.

Oakle chuckled, a warm, creaky sound like dry leaves skittering across grass. “If we think about the days, we can make a watering plan for your thirsty friends.”

Benji’s heart did a happy little leap. “A plan. Yes.”

Dot fluttered down onto a smooth, flat stone near his feet, perfect for drawing. “Write it down. Then you will not forget.”

He rummaged in his gardening bag and pulled out a smooth fallen twig. He began to draw in the soft, dark earth on the stone. Seven neat little boxes, side by side.

“For Monday,” he announced, and wrote a big M in the first box. “For Tuesday,” a T. He drew and wrote for Wednesday (a W), Thursday (a Th), Friday (an F), Saturday (an S), and a Su for Sunday. Seven little boxes, ready.

Dot pointed a tiny leg toward the pea plants, who were indeed looking parched. “Peas on Monday.”

Benji smiled a big gardener’s smile. “Peas on Monday. Hooray for Monday.” He looked at the proud petunias, petals drooping ever so slightly. “Petunias can have their drink on Tuesday. Twice as nice, Tuesday.”

They went on, Benji drawing and Dot suggesting, assigning each plant its own watering day. The giggling geraniums, who always seemed to chuckle when they got a drink, went down for Wednesday. The cheerful chives, who smelled so lovely when you brushed them, were for Thursday. The tall, sunny sunflowers, who always seemed to be smiling at the sky, got Friday. The bouncy beans, who loved to stretch their stems, were scheduled for Saturday. The shy little strawberries, hiding under their leaves, were a sweet surprise for Sunday.

“Hooray,” cheered Dot, doing a wiggle-dance on the stone, her seven spots seeming to bounce.

Benji looked at his garden chart, the earth-boxes filled with plant names and drink days. A fluttery feeling moved in his tummy, like a tiny butterfly exploring. “Thank you, Dot. Thank you, Oakle.”

He grabbed his watering can, filled it with cool, clear water, and skipped to the peas. “Moist on Monday,” he sang, and gave them a long drink. The soil went from dusty to dark. The pea leaves lifted a little, as if they had remembered their job.

The next morning he came back with the can already full. The proud petunias got their turn. Their petals perked up as if to say thank you. Benji tapped Tuesday’s box with the twig so the mark would stay.

He walked the rows with Dot on his shoulder. Wednesday waited for geraniums. Thursday smelled already of chives. Friday’s sunflowers tracked the light. Saturday’s beans leaned toward the path. Sunday’s strawberries stayed shy under their leaves, but he knew where they were.

“It is so much easier when we know the days,” he told Dot, who was busy counting her spots again, just for fun. He did not make a speech about friendship blooming. He hung the twig on a nail by the potting bench, where the stone-chart could be seen from the gate.

Oakle rustled his leaves, a sound like gentle applause. “The days help us line up our jobs,” he whispered. “Water when it is a plant’s day. Rest when it is not.”

Benji grinned, as bright as his sunflowers. He wiped the can’s spout and set it by Monday’s peas, ready for the week to turn again. Dot settled on the M box and counted to seven, slowly, as if the spots and the days had agreed to keep each other honest.
